facts.statement: Researchers created a mouse line where rod cells in the eye produce a glowing marker that lights up when glutamate is released.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The study tracked how much glutamate these rod cells let out under both dim and bright lighting conditions.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: When the researchers flashed light at the rods, the glowing marker dimmed, showing that the cells released less glutamate.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The pattern of glutamate release changed slowly, with its strength dropping off as the light flickered faster between 1 and 10 times per second.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The rod cells released glutamate in random bursts at a steady pace of 20 to 40 tiny packets per second, whether the light was dim or bright.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: A second electrical measurement method confirmed a similar release speed of about 38 packets per second.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Because the release speed stays the same across different light levels, the rod cells pass on their light-adjustment signals to the next neurons in the eye without distortion.
facts.subject: animals
